summary:
Konya stands within the national framework of Turkey, and the danger a trans visitor faces there is set by that framework rather than by any local instrument. No Konya-specific statute, incident, or court case is documented in the sources consulted for this entry; the findings below apply country-wide.

Turkey presents a structured and documented danger to trans visitors. Under a stated policy of protecting "the family" and "public morals", a leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package was reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. It would amend the penal code to imprison conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality for up to three years, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies for up to four years.

The same draft would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care, including surgery, from 18 to 25, and condition it on permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, and trans people receiving care deemed illegal up to three years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it. Human Rights Watch warns the measure would push treatment underground and expose people to arrest and pretrial detention. It had not been enacted when reported, and its pending status has not stopped authorities acting as though equivalent prohibitions were already in force.

Kaos GL's 2025 monitoring found that hostility toward LGBTI+ people in Turkey became explicit state policy. "Year of the Family" instructions were issued to public institutions, one LGBTI+ association was closed with criminal cases opened against eleven of its members, and artistic events were cancelled or banned. The same review recorded six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings, with trans people the most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations against 51 the previous year, roughly 313 violations overall, about two and a half times the 2024 total, 299 detention decisions, and freedom-of-expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

Street-level enforcement supplies the practical dimension. Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women in 2025 in the Beyoğlu district and held them for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release; one detainee reported that no fines were issued but the women were documented anyway, with enforcement applied before any new law had passed. Foreign visitors stopped at such checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk where appearance does not match the passport gender marker. Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention. Every document interaction is an occasion on which papers can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Turkey is lethal and state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, a change that risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.

Prison conditions govern any prolonged contact with the authorities. Trans prisoners in Turkey are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities; a transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, with accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reporting four transgender inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before, delayed medical staff, prosecutors entering two days later, and witnesses not interviewed. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025. A Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and ILGA World data documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, binary administration with no staff training on LGBT needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints that are ineffective and can attract further violence.
tangentialFactors:
Across the national monitoring data, every tracked indicator moved in the same direction at once: detentions roughly two and a half times the prior year, torture and ill-treatment up from 51 to 89, and freedom-of-expression violations up from 216 to 540. The simultaneity of those increases points to an enforcement posture rather than isolated episodes.

The draft penal-code package is a comparison point for how pending measures are already shaping conduct. Reported as unenacted in October 2025, it nevertheless appears alongside documented enforcement of the restrictions it proposes, which distinguishes the Turkish position from jurisdictions where an unpassed bill has no operational effect.

Istanbul supplies the clearest illustration of the pattern rather than a separate local regime. The stops, station detentions and identity-document demands recorded there in 2025 show the mechanism a trans visitor would meet at a checkpoint in Konya as readily as in Beyoğlu.

The state framework also rests on a long documented baseline. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, recorded continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people, and is cited as evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 still present in 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

Residents face a closed association and criminal proceedings: Kaos GL's 2025 review records one LGBTI+ association shut down with criminal cases against eleven of its members, alongside "Year of the Family" instructions issued to public institutions and the cancellation or banning of artistic events.

The draft package, if enacted, would bind residents more tightly than visitors in one respect: healthcare professionals performing gender-affirming interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, while trans people receiving care deemed illegal would face up to three years, alongside the 25-and-over age floor and infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions.

Transition care is already administratively constrained. The Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following the Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular, requires e-reports and removes the "other" option from hospital records, which profiles trans patients in official documentation.

Prisoners are placed by registered sex, a rule confirmed when a trans man was reported held in a women's prison. The death of the transgender prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 drew demands for an independent investigation from rights groups coordinated through Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025 by Sevda Karaca. Prison administration for LGBT detainees operates on a binary, heteronormative basis with no policy or staff training to identify their needs, and complaints mechanisms are ineffective and can attract further violence, according to the Prison Insider profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Konya-specific statute, incident, enforcement figure, or court case is documented in the sources consulted for this entry. Everything above is stated at national scope, and whether Konya police or prosecutors apply the documented checkpoint and detention practice at local rates is unresolved on the available material.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved beyond its reported position in October 2025: Human Rights Watch described it as a leaked draft that had not been passed, and no later source in the inventory confirms enactment or withdrawal.

The inventory contains no Konya Provincial Health Directorate circular and no local reporting on how the Health Ministry's September 2025 e-report requirement has been implemented in Konya's hospitals. The Kayseri circular is the nearest documented provincial analogue.

Whether the Kaos GL violation counts include any incidents occurring in Konya is not stated in the source; the totals are reported nationally without a provincial breakdown.
